Evaluating Temporal Reasoning in Large Language Models

Event Temporal Relation Extraction with Allen’s Interval Algebra, Logical Consistency, and Relative Time in Narratives

01 / Overview

Abstract

Understanding a narrative means knowing how every event relates in time to every other, yet large language models (LLMs) are mostly tested on isolated event pairs or coarse labels. We ask five LLMs to reconstruct the complete network of Allen's 13 interval relations for 360 English narratives whose events are placed relative to one another rather than by dates, and evaluate the outputs under a pre-registered protocol for agreement with our gold annotations, converse consistency and logical satisfiability. End to end, the best model clearly beats trivial baselines on macro-F1, our primary metric, yet under our pre-registered parser no model matches the accuracy of always answering before, which the skewed labels inflate. Most of that accuracy gap is a parsing artifact: formatting errors in large matrices cost whole rows, and a post hoc parser that recovers the determined cells of malformed rows raises coverage from 0.60 to 0.84 and closes the gap to the baseline for the best model. On the cells they do answer, models recover precedence and containment but rarely overlap, and they fail most on flashbacks, where both the narration and the event list present the later event first. Logical consistency varies widely yet says little about agreement with gold: enforcing it raises accuracy mainly by filling empty cells, and is beaten there by the trivial control of guessing the majority label. Reliable structured output and robust handling of relative time are prerequisites for temporal reasoning over whole narratives.

02 / Task & approach

From a narrative to a complete temporal network

Given a passage and a list of events quoted from it, a model assigns one of Allen’s 13 interval relations to every ordered pair. The output is a complete n × n matrix, rather than a set of isolated pairwise answers.

01 / INPUT

Passage + event list

Events are verbatim spans. Time is expressed primarily through relative relations, rather than dates.

02 / OUTPUT

Full relation matrix

One relation per ordered pair, with a dash on the diagonal. Both directions are requested.

03 / EVALUATION

Three complementary readings

Gold agreement, converse consistency, and exact satisfiability through endpoint constraints.

03 / Main results

Output fidelity shapes end-to-end performance

The best model reaches 0.270 macro-F1 under the pre-registered parser. No model matches the accuracy of always answering before.

These measures tell different stories. The majority relation accounts for 60.7% of scored pairs, inflating the accuracy of a trivial baseline. Macro-F1 gives each of the 13 relations equal weight and is the paper’s primary metric.

Malformed rows remove otherwise usable answers

Under strict parsing, a row with an unaccepted number of symbols becomes unusable. Coverage ranges from 2.4% to 60.0% across all five models; Mistral-Nemo produces almost no usable cells and is excluded from the paper’s subsequent main analyses.

Answered cells reveal a different picture

DeepSeek and GPT-6-Luna reach 0.753 and 0.728 accuracy on the cells they answer, exceeding always before on those same subsets. These are conditional diagnostics: answered cells disproportionately come from shorter passages.

Coherent networks can still be wrong

Among the four models with non-trivial coverage, converse violations range from 0.3% to 37.6%. Enforcing consistency helps mainly by filling missing cells, with answered-cell accuracy changing by at most 2.5 percentage points.

Models recover precedence and containment more readily than overlap. Flashbacks are especially difficult when both narration order and the event list put the later event first.

A post hoc parser recovers much of the missing output

The recovery parser retains cells whose positions are determined despite a malformed row, then fills gaps from the model’s own mirror cell. It uses the same stored outputs and never contradicts a strictly parsed cell.

Passage size and the cost of a full matrix

The 33 passages with more than 40 events contain 39.5% of all scored pairs. DeepSeek’s macro-F1 falls from 0.494 on passages with 8–15 events to 0.132 above 40 events. In a regression including standardised event count and word count, event count is significant for all four main models (p < 0.001); word count is not (p ≥ 0.052). Event count is also confounded with narrative complexity.

Logical validity and the repair control

DeepSeek has 212 satisfiable networks among 242 with a complete upper triangle. Qwen has 19 among 114. A logically valid output, however, can disagree with gold: DeepSeek is still wrong on 24.7% of its answered cells.

A control that simply fills every missing cell with before outperforms the best-found consistent repair for every main model on both accuracy and macro-F1. For DeepSeek, filling reaches 0.702 accuracy, compared with 0.591 for repair using both triangles.

Relation extraction, composition, and flashbacks

An error is composition-available when two correctly predicted premises through an intermediate event uniquely determine its gold relation. Only 4.4% of DeepSeek’s errors on pairs at least two sentences apart meet this criterion; the other models reach at most 2.8%. On correctly answered cells, such paths are available 66.2%–78.1% of the time. The paper interprets this contrast as evidence that extracting the premises from text is the dominant difficulty.

Most answered errors are not one-endpoint near misses: those account for 23.8%–33.4% of errors. Severity 2 is the most frequent class for DeepSeek and GPT-6-Luna, at 43.5% and 42.0%.

On answered before/after pairs, DeepSeek is accurate at 0.909–0.923 when at most one of the two surface cues contradicts chronology, but falls to 0.739 when both list order and narration order do so. GPT-6-Luna reaches 0.711 in that joint-reversal condition.

Read the statistical qualification and algebraic context

The cue interaction, controlling for sentence distance, is significant for DeepSeek, Gemini, and Qwen, but not GPT-6-Luna (p = 0.197). Controlling for the gold relation on before/after pairs removes the list cue by construction, because the two indicators are collinear. Non-linearity and passage size are partly confounded; these analyses are observational.

Allen’s relations form six converse pairs and the self-converse equal relation. Of 169 basic-relation compositions, 97 yield one relation. For example, meets ∘ meets = before, whereas overlaps ∘ overlaps permits before, meets, or overlaps. The paper enumerates the complete composition table in its algebra appendix.

Basic-relation networks translate to endpoint comparisons, so exact satisfiability reduces to cycle detection after merging equal endpoints. The minimum-change repair is a separate combinatorial search problem. Error severity counts disagreements among four endpoint comparisons: start–start, start–end, end–start, and end–end.

Source: Results, “What kind of errors” and “Narration order and list order”; appendices “Allen’s Interval Algebra”, “Controls for the Repair and Composition Analyses”, and “Error Severity and Passage Size”.

Cross-model agreement and additional diagnostics

On 1,778 pairs answered by all five models, Fleiss’ κ is 0.219. DeepSeek and GPT-6-Luna have the strongest pairwise agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.652 on cells both answer). A five-model plurality vote reaches 0.561 accuracy and 0.242 macro-F1. On 37.8% of pairs, no model is correct; an oracle selecting any correct model reaches 0.622 accuracy.

Errors are moderately concentrated on individual events. In passages with at least five errors, the event associated with the most errors accounts for an average of 31.2% of DeepSeek’s errors and 29.5% of GPT-6-Luna’s. Same-sentence pairs have the lowest macro-F1 for every model; nearby pairs contain more fine relations. The duration flag makes little difference to DeepSeek’s accuracy (0.458 with it, 0.445 without).

05 / Data & protocol

A controlled evaluation of relative time

The narrative corpus

The authors wrote and annotated the fictional English passages for this study. Most are personal narratives set in Bangladesh; others include non-linear literary pieces, procedural and engineering timelines, and short scenes.

Evaluated passages
360
Total selected events

Passages mentioning a year
or a day of the month

Evaluation protocol

  1. The prompt, parser, primary metric, gold data, and seven hypotheses were frozen before querying. This was a self-administered freeze without a third-party timestamp.
  2. Each model received the same prompt and returned the full matrix. Calls were repeated only after transport failures.
  3. The upper triangle measures agreement with gold; the lower triangle tests converses; endpoint constraints test satisfiability exactly.
  4. Confidence intervals use 1,000 passage-level bootstrap resamples. Holm correction applies within the pre-registered hypothesis family.
Corpus composition and temporal-expression profile

One passage was excluded because its event list assigned the same identifier to different events. A further 101 longer, unannotated passages are not evaluated. Of the 360 included passages, 90 are fully linear and 270 are non-linear; 107 have more than 20% reversed before/after pairs.

The corpus contains 102,746 words. Its temporal-expression profile was measured with regular expressions, not human annotations. Absolute anchors are years or days of a month; partial anchors include weekdays, month names without a year, and clock times. Offsets, deictic phrases, connectives, and past perfect provide relative cues.

Source: “Task and Data” and “Relative Time in the Corpus”. The paper discusses missing shared time axes, reference resolution, narrative bias, implicit boundaries, and chained offsets as sources of difficulty.

Model settings, output parsing, and experimental cost

All five models were accessed through OpenRouter. Reasoning effort was medium where supported; Mistral-Nemo has no reasoning parameter. Temperature 0 and seed 20261006 were sent where accepted. GPT-6-Luna does not accept temperature and used the provider default. The output limit was 65,536 tokens, or 16,384 for Mistral-Nemo.

Read the frozen prompt reproduced in the paper

The item-specific placeholders below are reproduced from the TeX source. The displayed three-event matrix is a format illustration, not a scored example.

===== SYSTEM =====
You are an expert annotator of temporal relations between events described in text.
===== USER =====
Read the passage and the list of events taken from it. Each event is identified by an ID and
by the words that describe it in the passage.

Your task: for every ordered pair of different events (X, Y), decide which ONE of Allen's 13
interval relations holds between the time interval of event X and the time interval of event
Y, according to the passage. Every pair must receive exactly one relation; if the passage does
not state it explicitly, choose the most plausible one.

The 13 relations (read as "X relation Y"):
<   X before Y: X ends before Y starts (there is a gap between them).
>   X after Y: X starts after Y ends (there is a gap between them).
m   X meets Y: X ends exactly when Y starts.
mi  X met by Y: X starts exactly when Y ends.
o   X overlaps Y: X starts before Y starts, and X ends after Y starts but before Y ends.
oi  X overlapped by Y: Y starts before X starts, and Y ends after X starts but before X ends.
s   X starts Y: X and Y start together, and X ends before Y ends.
si  X started by Y: X and Y start together, and X ends after Y ends.
d   X during Y: X starts after Y starts and ends before Y ends.
di  X contains Y: Y starts after X starts and ends before X ends.
f   X finishes Y: X and Y end together, and X starts after Y starts.
fi  X finished by Y: X and Y end together, and X starts before Y starts.
=   X equals Y: X and Y start together and end together.

PASSAGE:
"""
<passage text>
"""

EVENTS (<n> events):
E1: <verbatim span>
...

OUTPUT FORMAT
Write the complete <n> x <n> relation matrix between the tags <matrix> and </matrix>.
- Write exactly one line per event, in the order of the event list above.
- Each line starts with the row event's ID followed by a colon, then <n> symbols separated by
  single spaces.
- The k-th symbol in the row of event X is the relation of X to the k-th event of the list (X
  relation that event). Column order: E1 E2 ... En
- Use "-" on the diagonal (the cell of an event with itself).
- Use only these symbols: < > m mi o oi s si d di f fi = -
- Write nothing else inside the tags.

E1: - < m

Research context, ethics, and directions for future work

The paper situates the task alongside temporal-link annotation, dense event-graph extraction, global consistency methods, and temporal benchmarks for language models. Its focus is the complete fine-grained Allen network of each narrative, evaluated jointly for gold agreement, converse consistency, and satisfiability. Related Work and the bibliography in the paper provide the full literature discussion.

The passages are author-written fiction, describe no real individuals, and contain no personally identifying information. The authors produced the annotations and screened every passage; no crowdworkers or other participants were involved. The paper discloses AI assistance with code and writing, with the authors retaining responsibility for design, testing, and reported results.

The conclusion proposes measuring run-to-run variation, testing alternative output formats, auditing model–gold disagreements, and extending evaluation to spatial relations. The paper cautions against unsupervised use of these complete-network outputs in sensitive timeline applications.

Source: Related Work, Discussion, Conclusion, and Ethical Considerations. Full references, algebra tables, supplementary figures, and the complete PDF are also available in the technical companion and materials sections below.

06 / Scope & limitations

How to read these results

Protocol-specific performance

The study uses one prompt, one full-matrix output format, and one run per model. Confidence intervals capture variation across passages, not run-to-run variation. Alternative prompting, structured outputs, or reasoning budgets may change the results.

Known annotation issues

Inter-annotator agreement has not been measured across the full corpus. Thirty-two gold networks are unsatisfiable, with a systematic issue involving meets. A further 665 model–gold disagreements remain unaudited; model consensus alone cannot establish an annotation error.

The corpus is English and limited in genre. Human-level agreement remains unknown. Consistent repairs are the best found within a time limit and are not always proven optimal. See the paper’s Limitations section for the complete discussion.

07 / Technical companion

Methods, statistical detail, and complete paper figures

The sections below complement the main results with the paper’s methodological, algebraic, and supplementary detail. Numerical claims follow the local paper source and released result tables; observational results and post hoc analyses retain their qualifications.

Task motivation, contributions, and related work

Reading a narrative requires a coherent timeline even when an application mentioned late in a passage “had actually been shortlisted in July”, before an interview narrated earlier. Allen’s interval algebra distinguishes precedence, contact, overlap, containment, shared starts, shared finishes, and equality. Complete matrices expose failures that isolated pairs and coarse labels can conceal.

The paper contributes a pre-registered complete-network evaluation; a diagnosis of formatting losses under single-shot free-text prompting; evidence that logical consistency and gold agreement are distinct; and analysis of overlap, flashback, event-count, endpoint-severity, and composition failures. Its novelty claim concerns complete 13-relation networks from narratives under this evaluation regime.

Temporal relations in text.

TimeML and the TempEval campaigns established event and temporal-link annotation and evaluation [4, 5], and [15] proposed closure-based temporal awareness scores. Because annotating all pairs is quadratic, early corpora labelled few links; dense and exhaustive schemes such as TimeBank-Dense [10], TIMELINE [16] and EventFull [17] cover more of each document's graph, and [18] showed that missing inter-sentence links distort evaluation. MATRES restricts judgments to start points to raise agreement [11], and other work anchors events on a time line or on continuous scales [19, 20]. Narrative corpora add causal structure [21, 22]. Our setting differs from all of these in requiring the complete set of 13 Allen relations for every event pair of a narrative.

Global consistency in extraction.

Temporal relations constrain each other through symmetry and transitivity, and classical systems enforce these constraints with integer linear programming or structured learning [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28]. Reasoning in the full interval algebra is NP-hard, whereas point-based fragments are tractable [2, 3]; [29] exploit the same endpoint view to define relations as comparisons of start and end points. We use an endpoint encoding to test satisfiability exactly and to compute minimum-change repairs.

LLMs and temporal reasoning.

Zero-shot ChatGPT lags supervised extractors on temporal relations [30], broad benchmarks report clear gaps between LLMs and humans on ordering, duration and temporal arithmetic [7, 8], and TNR evaluates numerical and relational temporal reasoning jointly [31]. [9] find that LLMs lag behind humans and are frequently self-inconsistent, [32] identify narrative and tense biases, and [33] and [34] show that answers change when the same ordering question is rephrased. ChronoSense evaluates Allen relations between pairs of events and finds uneven performance across relations [14], QSTRBench probes composition in qualitative calculi [35], and TRACE frames Allen reasoning as constraint satisfaction with synthetic difficulty control [36]. Closest to our work, [12] and [37] generate whole temporal graphs with prompting, and [13] show that consistent clinical predictions can still be wrong. These studies use coarse label sets, pairwise questions or synthetic inputs; we evaluate the full 13-relation network of narratives, with converse and satisfiability analyses of the same outputs.

Corpus structure, gold-label support, and baseline definitions

Scoring uses one unordered pair represented by the upper-triangle cell i < j in event-list order, whereas the requested output contains both ordered directions. The text-order baseline predicts < if the first event’s span occurs first in the passage and > otherwise; the always-before baseline predicts < for every scored pair.

Among 80,406 gold before/after pairs, 23.9% are narrated in reverse chronological order. The event list follows narration order in 164 passages; pairwise list and narration orders agree for 93.3% of all pairs. On average, 88.7% of a passage’s gold pairs are derivable from two other gold relations in one composition step.

The 32 unsatisfiable gold networks contain 640 violating triples of the form A meets B, B meets C, A meets C; the third relation must instead be before. Gold agreement remains the scoring target, so a logically required answer can count as wrong. This is why gold agreement and validity are reported separately.

Counts use the first occurrence of each event identifier. Totals can be below 7,627 because some rows are absent. Wrong-length rows account for 18.3% of emitted rows for DeepSeek, 33.0% for GPT-6-Luna, 29.5% for Gemini, 42.3% for Qwen, and 93.5% for Mistral. DeepSeek and Gemini predominantly write too many symbols (86.7% and 81.3% of malformed rows); GPT-6-Luna predominantly writes too few (87.2%).

Truncation is uncommon overall but substantial on the largest passages. Averaged over passages rather than cells, coverage ranges from 85.4% for DeepSeek to 66.7% for Qwen. The primary figure remains cell-weighted coverage because the evaluation target is the corpus of pairs.

For recovery, let a row’s length differ from n by k, with its dash at its own event position. Left anchoring assigns token j to column j; right anchoring assigns token j + k to that column. Accept a cell where both readings agree; abstain otherwise. Runs of identical symbols allow many cells to be recovered. A second pass fills a remaining gap from the model’s converse mirror cell. Neither pass overwrites a strictly parsed cell, and agreement on jointly filled cells is 1.000 for every model.

Endpoint satisfiability, both repair variants, and composition controls

Map each answered relation to comparisons of its four endpoints, merge endpoints required to be equal, and check for a cycle containing a strict inequality. A basic-relation network is satisfiable exactly when there is no such cycle. Missing cells impose no constraint.

The repair returns a complete satisfiable network maximising agreement with answered cells within the time limit. Variant (i) uses upper-triangle answers; variant (ii) also treats each converse-converted lower-triangle answer as a second vote for the pair. The optimisation has no per-label confidence scores. Preserving answered cells is partly a consequence of its objective.

Among answered errors on reversed pairs, 73.9%–76.5% follow narration order for DeepSeek, GPT-6-Luna, and Gemini, compared with 47.0% for Qwen. A passage-clustered logistic GEE controlling for gold relation and sentence distance finds no significant reversal effect (odds ratios 0.65–2.19; all p ≥ 0.058). However, on scored before/after pairs, gold after is exactly the indicator that list order reverses chronology, so that control removes the list cue.

The cue-interaction specification is correct ~ list × narration + sentence distance, on answered before/after pairs, with a logistic link, independence working correlation, and passage-clustered robust standard errors.

Gemini instead falls whenever the list reverses chronology (0.375 and 0.232), regardless of narration. DeepSeek’s passage-level macro-F1 is 0.393 on fully linear passages and 0.204 on strongly non-linear passages; size and non-linearity are partly confounded.

Of four endpoint comparisons, end-of-first versus start-of-second is wrong in 68.3%–74.3% of answered errors. Severity-4 errors account for 19.4% of DeepSeek errors and 30.0% of Qwen errors. Severity-1 near misses account for 83.6% of DeepSeek’s gold-overlaps errors and 65.5% of its gold-meets errors, but just 4.0% of its gold-after errors.

In passages with at least five errors, the most error-prone event accounts for more than half of errors in 12.2% of DeepSeek passages and 11.4% of GPT-6-Luna passages. Same/adjacent-sentence pairs have higher error rates than distant pairs (DeepSeek: 0.608 versus 0.510), partly because fine relations are more common nearby. DeepSeek accuracy by first-event position is 0.452 at the beginning, 0.433 in the middle, and 0.472 at the end; this small pattern is untested.

Passage-level macro-F1 correlates with event count (Spearman ρ from −0.57 for DeepSeek to −0.68 for Qwen) and word count (−0.41 to −0.52). Generated-row accuracy declines from first to last decile for GPT-6-Luna (0.410 to 0.291) and Qwen (0.244 to 0.164); DeepSeek shows no such decline.

DeepSeek and GPT-6-Luna’s mutual κ of 0.652 exceeds their answered-cell agreement with gold (0.575 and 0.523). On 291 logically impossible gold-meets A–C chain pairs, models reproduce gold at most 8.6% of the time (DeepSeek), while logically required before predictions range from 7.9% (Qwen) to 26.1% (Gemini). DeepSeek macro-F1 on the 32 inconsistent-gold passages is 0.200, versus 0.290 on the rest. Of 665 consensus disagreements, 182 are gold meets versus consensus before; these remain unaudited.

Relative time: definitions, all seven challenges, and anchor analysis

Absolute anchors identify a year or day of a month. Partial anchors name weekdays, months without years, or clock times. Offsets specify distance from another time (“twelve days later”, “three months ago”); deictic expressions use a reference point (“the following week”); connectives include before, after, when, while, until, since, and by then. Past perfect uses had plus a participle to place an event before the current narrative reference time.

Of 38 absolute-anchor mentions, 35 are bare years and three are days of a month. Absolute anchors are absent from 338 passages (93.9%); 157 passages (43.6%) contain no calendar expression of any kind. At event level, 4.1% occur in a sentence with an absolute anchor, 24.0% with any calendar expression, and 58.0% with at least one relative cue. All these counts use heuristic regular expressions.

  1. No shared axis. Absolute times can locate each event independently; relative positions depend on chains of relations. Although 88.7% of gold pairs are one-step derivable, models rarely have correct premises where they err.
  2. Explicit times are scarce in other corpora too. The cited literature reports time-expression links for about 20% of TimeBank-Dense events, and imprecise temporal information for 58% of TimeBank events. This corpus has absolute anchors near only 4% of events.
  3. Dependence on explicit anchors. The paper cites biography experiments in which replacing dates with relative expressions reduces ordering accuracy for humans and most models; it also discusses heuristic shortcuts on numerical–relational benchmarks.
  4. Reference resolution. “Two weeks after” needs a reference event; past perfect needs a reference time. “On Tuesday” and “that Friday” need a week context. The cited TimeBank signal study finds that “in” is temporal only 13.3% of the time.
  5. Narration-order default. Readers and models often interpret successive clauses chronologically. Tense and connectives must override that default in flashbacks; past perfect occurs in 83.3% of these passages.
  6. Implicit interval boundaries. Allen labels depend on starts and ends, which narratives often leave to commonsense inference. Shared endpoints distinguish meets, starts, and finishes; overlaps instead depends on the strict order of four endpoints.
  7. Arithmetic along offset chains. Resolving “twelve days later” and “two weeks after” can require adding durations along multiple links, a weakness discussed in the cited temporal benchmarks.

Calendar-bearing event sentences do not produce higher answered-cell accuracy in the reported comparison: when both events have a calendar expression versus neither, DeepSeek scores 0.720 versus 0.748, and GPT-6-Luna 0.662 versus 0.728. Most anchors are partial, and the comparison is observational because anchors cluster by passage type.

Efficiency uses unrounded macro-F1 and USD cost from the released reliability-and-cost CSV. For Mistral this is 0.064665, rounded to 0.065; the paper’s setup table instead reports 0.075. Retried-call counts are unchanged.

Requests were streamed. DeepSeek generated 7.46 million completion tokens, mostly reasoning tokens, versus 1.93 million for GPT-6-Luna. GPT-6-Luna has the highest recorded macro-F1 per dollar; DeepSeek has the highest absolute quality at about four times its run cost. These describe this experiment, not current pricing.

OpenRouter can route a model’s requests to different providers: DeepSeek’s calls were served by five. The paper makes no model-scale or architecture claims because attributes such as parameter counts are not published for all models. Temperature defaults, the single run, one frozen prompt, full-matrix output, and medium reasoning effort limit generalisation. Confidence intervals measure passage sampling only.

There is no measured full-corpus inter-annotator agreement or human ceiling. Meets is the least reliable gold label, including outside the 32 inconsistent passages; meets/met-by cover 4.3% of pairs. Absorbing them into before/after preserves the primary model ranking. Duration and temporal-expression flags are heuristic. Model-selected answered subsets, solver time limits, and observational confounding also limit interpretation.

The discussion distinguishes three claims: incomplete end-to-end output, stronger conditional agreement on answered cells, and weak correspondence between logical consistency and correctness. Asking for both triangles doubles output exposure. Timeline construction before labelling is suggested as a possible reading intervention, rather than established as an effective method in this experiment. Future work includes repeated runs, alternative formats, auditing disagreements, and spatial relations.

The author-written fictional corpus, annotations, stored responses, analysis code, and paper source are released under MIT. The authors report no restrictive third-party data dependencies, no human participants or crowdworkers, and author screening of every passage. They disclose AI assistance with code and writing and retain responsibility for the study. The paper cautions against unsupervised sensitive-domain timeline deployment.

All 13 endpoint signatures and the full 13 × 13 composition table

Allen’s qualitative interval algebra was introduced for natural-language understanding and planning. Its primitive is a proper interval, with start strictly before end. It encodes no duration. The 13 basic relations are jointly exhaustive and pairwise disjoint, with six converse pairs and self-converse equality.

<beforex⁺ < y⁻<<<<

mmeetsx⁺ = y⁻<<=<
mimet-byy⁺ = x⁻>=>>
ooverlapsx⁻ < y⁻ < x⁺ < y⁺<<><
oioverlapped-byy⁻ < x⁻ < y⁺ < x⁺><>>
sstartsx⁻ = y⁻; x⁺ < y⁺=<><
sistarted-byx⁻ = y⁻; y⁺ < x⁺=<>>
dduringy⁻ < x⁻; x⁺ < y⁺><><

fifinished-byx⁺ = y⁺; x⁻ < y⁻<<>=
=equalx⁻ = y⁻; x⁺ = y⁺=<>=

Here ss compares x⁻ with y⁻, se compares x⁻ with y⁺, es compares x⁺ with y⁻, and ee compares x⁺ with y⁺. Only 13 of the 3⁴ = 81 possible sign patterns can arise for two proper intervals. Error severity is the number of differing comparisons: meets versus before differs only in es; before versus after differs in all four.

full means all 13 relations; conc means the nine relations sharing time: o, oi, s, si, d, di, f, fi, =. Of 169 basic compositions, 97 are single-valued. Meets composed with meets yields before; overlaps composed with overlaps yields before, meets, or overlaps. The paper derives this table by enumerating concrete integer-endpoint configurations.

Disjunctions produce 2¹³ = 8,192 general relations. Satisfiability for general interval networks is NP-complete, and path consistency alone is insufficient in general. The paper discusses ORD-Horn and other tractable subclasses and fuzzy extensions. Here each answered pair has a basic relation, so exact satisfiability reduces to a polynomial-time endpoint-graph check over 2n endpoints; minimum-change repair remains a separate combinatorial search.
